abstract.p: This paper contributes to the trend of building semantic representations and exploring the relations between a language and the world it represents. We analyse alternative approaches to semantic representation, focusing on methodology of determining meaning categories, their arrangement and granularity, and annotation consistency and reliability. Using the task of semantic classification of circumstantial meanings within the Prague Dependency Treebank framework, we present our principles for analyzing meaning categories. Compared with the discussed projects, the unique aspect of our approach is its focus on how a language, in its structure, reflects reality. We employ a twolevel classification: a higher, coarse-grained set of general semantic concepts (defined by questions: where, how, why, etc.) and a fine-grained set of circumstantial meanings based on datadriven analysis, reflecting meanings fixed in the language. We highlight that the inherent vagueness of linguistic meaning is crucial for capturing the limitless variety of the world but it can lead to label biases in datasets. Therefore, besides semantically clear categories, we also use fuzzy meaning categories. We support this position with a brief annotation experiment.
